Compare GLM fit and predictive error metrics

Source: R/model_performance.R
model_performance.Rd

Report AIC, BIC, response-scale RMSE and residual deviance for one or more fitted GLMs.

Usage

model_performance(...)

Arguments

...

One or more objects of class "glm".

Value

A data frame of class "model_performance", with columns:

Model

Name of the model object as passed to the function.

AIC

AIC value.

BIC

BIC value.

RMSE

Response-scale root mean squared error.

Residual_Deviance

Residual deviance.

Details

The following measures are reported:

AIC

Akaike information criterion, balancing likelihood fit and model complexity.

BIC

Bayesian information criterion, applying a stronger sample-size-dependent complexity penalty.

RMSE

Root mean squared error between observed and response-scale predicted values.

Residual_Deviance

Residual deviance of the fitted GLM, as returned by stats::deviance().

AIC, BIC and residual deviance describe in-sample fit. RMSE measures in-sample prediction error on the response scale, comparing observed responses with fitted values on the same rows used to estimate the model. It is unweighted and uses the same response scale as validate_performance(). None of these metrics establishes out-of-sample predictive performance.

For a Poisson frequency model with offset(log(exposure)), the fitted values are expected claim counts for each observation's exposure. RMSE therefore measures error in claim counts, not claim frequencies per unit exposure. For binomial GLMs it measures errors on the probability scale.

Compare models on the same response, estimation records, weights and offsets. For residual deviance, also use the same model family.

The table does not select a pricing model automatically. In actuarial model assessment, statistical fit should be considered together with portfolio calibration, residual behaviour, coefficient stability, exposure by level and the practical interpretability of the resulting tariff structure.

The implementation is adapted from performance::model_performance().

See also

rmse(), validate_performance(), check_overdispersion(), check_residuals()

Author

Martin Haringa

Examples

portfolio <- as.data.frame(MTPL)
portfolio$zip <- factor(portfolio$zip)
m1 <- glm(nclaims ~ zip + offset(log(exposure)), family = poisson(),
          data = portfolio)
m2 <- glm(nclaims ~ zip + age_policyholder + offset(log(exposure)),
          family = poisson(), data = portfolio)
# RMSE is in claim counts for these exposure-offset models.
model_performance(m1, m2)
#> # Comparison of Model Performance Indices
#> 
#> Model |    AIC    |    BIC    | RMSE  | Residual_Deviance 
#> ------+-----------+-----------+-------+------------------ 
#>    m1 | 23188.832 | 23222.068 | 0.364 |         16327.135 
#>    m2 | 22967.939 | 23009.484 | 0.362 |         16104.242
